slides.text:
Household income and
reported diabetes
Does the income gap remain after accounting
for age and BMI?

Strong Tiger · Tiger, Harry, yingcheLiu and Reiyume

Cleaned 2015 BRFSS sample · University of Edinburgh · 24 October 2026

1 / 13

slides.title: Data and outcome
slides.text:
Data and outcome

253,680 adult survey responses · 21 indicators

Source: cleaned 2015 CDC BRFSS files, linked through UCI
Outcome: reported diabetes, verified against the original three-category file
Age and income are categories, not exact ages or dollar amounts
202,943 training / 50,737 test records

No survey weights in this extract: our results describe this sample.

Sources: CDC 2015 documentation; UCI dataset 891; Teboul's original files

2 / 13

slides.title: Observed income differences
slides.text:
Observed income differences

Lowest income: 24.3% · Highest income: 8.0%

Training sample. Points show observed proportions; bars show 95% Wilson intervals.

3 / 13

slides.title: Making an adjusted comparison
slides.text:
Making an adjusted comparison

The income groups differ in age and BMI.

Characteristic	Income < $10,000	Income $75,000+
Aged 60 or older	41.4%	36.5%
Mean BMI	29.7	27.6

Logistic regression: income band + age category + curved BMI term + sex

We compare income bands using the same age, BMI and sex distribution.

Income and age are categorical. BMI uses a natural cubic spline with 3 degrees of freedom.

4 / 13

slides.title: The adjusted income gap remains
slides.text:
The adjusted income gap remains

Lowest minus highest: 14.3 percentage points
95% model-based interval: 13.4-15.2 points

Standardised to the training sample's joint covariate distribution. Not a causal effect.

5 / 13

slides.title: Why 86% accuracy is not enough
slides.text:
Why 86% accuracy is not enough
Model	AUC	Accuracy	Sensitivity
Always predict no diabetes	0.500	86.1%	0.0%
Age + BMI + sex	0.750	86.0%	3.9%
Add income	0.768	86.1%	6.5%

Adding income improves ranking and probability error modestly.

At a 0.5 threshold, the model identifies only 6.5% of the diabetes cases.

Useful for describing group differences; not a validated screening rule.

Untouched test sample, n = 50,737. Sensitivity is the fraction of positive cases identified.

6 / 13

slides.title: Robustness of the income comparison
slides.text:
Robustness of the income comparison

Lowest versus highest income: adjusted odds ratio

Analysis	OR	95% model-based interval
Primary model	3.39	3.18 - 3.61
Linear BMI	3.46	3.25 - 3.68
Exclude prediabetes	3.52	3.30 - 3.75
Exclude BMI above 60	3.37	3.16 - 3.59

The association is similar under these three checks.

An odds ratio is not a probability ratio. Sensitivity checks do not eliminate confounding.

7 / 13

slides.title: What the findings support
slides.text:
What the findings support

A substantial income difference remains in this sample.

It deserves further investigation when discussing accessible health education and support.

The analysis cannot establish:

that changing income would cause the observed difference;
current national prevalence from selected 2015 responses;
an individual's diagnosis or the best service allocation.

Next step: newer survey data with weights and sampling design.

Backup: the outcome coding audit

All 253,680 rows and all 21 predictor columns were compared.

Original	Binary	Respondents
0: no diabetes / pregnancy only	0	213,703
1: prediabetes	0	4,631
2: diabetes	1	35,346

The binary positive class matches diabetes only, despite the website wording.

Direct comparison of the UCI CSV and the original three-category file. No predictor-row mismatches.
